we're working on reworking the layout of the main window.  Made a number of attempts to correct it on this branch but want to try some more serious changes.

I have these two options: Short version: the “mystery toolbar” is showing up because **any** `.toolbar { ... }` attached to *either* column of a `NavigationSplitView` contributes items to the **window toolbar** on macOS. In your code you hide the “automatic” toolbar and then re-add a `ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation)` inside the sidebar column, which forces SwiftUI to create a window toolbar region even if it contains just that one button. That’s why you’re seeing an extra bar. 

Below is a tight, Apple-docs-backed plan with two clean architectures. Pick one and it’ll eliminate the phantom bar and align you with current SwiftUI best practices.

---

# What you have today (relevant bits)

* `NavigationSplitView` with per-column toolbars:

  * Sidebar column: `.toolbar(.hidden, for: .automatic)` **and** a `ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation)` for the sidebar toggle.
  * Detail column: `.toolbar(.hidden, for: .automatic)`.
* Window is content-driven (`.windowResizability(.contentSize)`) and uses a custom “card” treatment for both columns.  

**Why this causes the ghost bar**

* On macOS, applying `.toolbar { ... }` to a view inside your scene populates the **window toolbar**; SwiftUI merges toolbar contributions across the hierarchy. So even one `ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation)` in a child view creates a window toolbar area. ([Apple Developer][1])

---

# Two solid fixes (choose one)

## Option A — “Zero-toolbar” window (no toolbar region at all)

**Goal:** Remove the window toolbar entirely and keep your toggle inside your own header UI.

**Why it’s correct**

* `NavigationSplitView` works fine as the root without a toolbar. Apple’s guidance: make it the scene’s root and only add a toolbar if you actually need toolbar commands. ([Apple Developer][2])
* HIG: Don’t show empty or vestigial toolbars; toolbars are for commands that act on the content. ([Apple Developer][3])

**Patch (minimal)**

1. **Remove** all column-level `.toolbar{}` from `ContentView` (both the `.hidden` lines and the `ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation)` button).

```diff
- .toolbar(.hidden, for: .automatic)
- .toolbar {
-   ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation) {
-     Button { withAnimation { columnVisibility.toggleSplitVisibility() } } {
-       Image(systemName: "sidebar.left")
-     }
-   }
- }
```

2. **Put the toggle button in your header** (it already fits your design system):

```swift
// In `headerWithoutComposeToggle` right-side button cluster:
Button {
    withAnimation { columnVisibility.toggleSplitVisibility() }
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "sidebar.left")
}
.buttonStyle(.borderless)
.help(columnVisibility == .all ? "Hide compose panel" : "Show compose panel")
```

3. (Optional, belt-and-suspenders) **Hide any window toolbar items at the scene level**:

```swift
// ContextifyApp.swift (on the Window scene)
.toolbarVisibility(.hidden, for: .windowToolbar)
```

This hides *items* if any stray view still contributes them. (Apple: “hide the window toolbar items on macOS.”) ([Apple Developer][4])

**Result:** No NSToolbar region is created; no “mystery” bar.

---

## Option B — “One real toolbar” (window-level, not per-column)

**Goal:** Keep a standard macOS toolbar (with a proper sidebar toggle), but make it **single-source** and window-scoped.

**Why it’s correct**

* Apple recommends attaching toolbars at an owning container (the split view or window), rather than scattering per-column items. This avoids flicker and role conflicts as columns appear/disappear. ([Apple Developer][5])
* Use the right **toolbar role** for a document/editor-style app (`.editor`) so SwiftUI arranges items appropriately on macOS. ([Apple Developer][6])

**Patch (minimal)**

1. **Remove all** column-level `.toolbar{}` modifiers (as in Option A step 1).

2. **Add one window-level toolbar** (attach to the split view *or* the outer `VStack`, not a column):

```swift
NavigationSplitView(columnVisibility: $columnVisibility) {
    // sidebar...
} detail: {
    // detail...
}
.toolbarRole(.editor) // macOS-friendly layout for commands
.toolbar {
    // A single, window-scoped sidebar toggle
    ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation) {
        Button {
            withAnimation { columnVisibility.toggleSplitVisibility() }
        } label: {
            Image(systemName: "sidebar.left")
        }
        .help(columnVisibility == .all ? "Hide sidebar" : "Show sidebar")
    }

    // (Optional) put search or other window-level commands here
}
```

3. (Optional) Pick a **window toolbar style** to match your look:

```swift
// ContextifyApp.swift, on the Window scene
.windowToolbarStyle(.unified)        // or .unifiedCompact / .expanded
```

(Apple: window toolbar styles tailor the title/toolbar chrome on macOS.) ([Apple Developer][7])

**Result:** A single, predictable NSToolbar with no ghost bars.

---

# Small cleanups (low-effort, best-practice)

* Replace the `DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter` in `presentToast` with `Task.sleep` to stay fully in Swift Concurrency:

```swift
Task { @MainActor in
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(autoDismissDuration))
    withAnimation { showToast = false }
}
```

(Apple’s modern pattern is `Task` + `Task.sleep` for UI delays.) ([Apple Developer][5])

* If/when you target macOS 26 only, you can adopt the new “Liquid Glass” visuals for a more native feel and potentially move away from custom “card” shadows. (WWDC25 sessions cover the new toolbar/visual language.) ([Apple Developer][8])

---

# Quick acceptance tests

1. Launch with **Option A**: no bar should appear above your content; the toggle in the header still hides/shows the compose sidebar.
2. Launch with **Option B**: one toolbar with a single sidebar toggle; toggling content or column visibility never creates a second bar.
3. Toggle the compose column with ⌥⌘S (your menu command) to verify parity regardless of toolbar choice. 

---

# Why this aligns with Apple’s guidance

* `NavigationSplitView` is intended as the root container; add toolbars **only** when you need a window toolbar for commands. ([Apple Developer][2])
* Toolbars belong to windows and scenes; contributions from child views are merged, so centralize them (or omit entirely). ([Apple Developer][1])
* Use `toolbarVisibility(.hidden, for: .windowToolbar)` to suppress window toolbar items when you don’t want a toolbar. ([Apple Developer][4])
* HIG advises against empty/vestigial bars; show one only if it has meaningful commands. ([Apple Developer][3])

If you want, I can generate a ready-to-apply diff for either option based on your current `ContentView.swift`/`ContextifyApp.swift` layout.

[1]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/toolbars?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Toolbars | Apple Developer Documentation"
[2]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/SwiftUI/NavigationSplitView?utm_source=chatgpt.com "NavigationSplitView | Apple Developer Documentation"
[3]: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toolbars?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Toolbars | Apple Developer Documentation"
[4]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/toolbarvisibility%28_%3Afor%3A%29?utm_source=chatgpt.com "toolbarVisibility(_:for:) | Apple Developer Documentation"
[5]: https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10148/?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Tailor macOS windows with SwiftUI - WWDC24 - Videos"
[6]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/toolbarrole%28_%3A%29?utm_source=chatgpt.com "toolbarRole(_:) | Apple Developer Documentation"
[7]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windowtoolbarstyle?utm_source=chatgpt.com "WindowToolbarStyle | Apple Developer Documentation"
